extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Kant / advanced readers of philosophy interested in metaphysics, teleology, and moral theology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Kantian standards about the distinction between theoretical cognition and practical (moral) faith, and the philosophical evaluation of proofs for God, freedom, and immortality in the Critique of Judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between things of fact and things of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects of history and geography, like everything which it is at least possible to know by the constitution of our cognitive faculties, belong not to things of faith but to things of fact. Only objects of pure Reason can be things of faith at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to decide whether a claim should be treated as empirical knowledge (testable, grounded in facts) or as a thing of faith (a practical postulate of Reason). Anti-pattern: treating empirical historical/geographical claims as matters of faith; conversely, trying to force supersensible Ideas into empirical verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith is moral (practical), not theoretical
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief in things of faith is a belief in a pure practical point of view, i.e. a moral faith, which proves nothing for theoretical pure rational cognition, but only for that which is practical and directed to the fulfilment of its duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about God, freedom, or immortality, distinguish whether the claim is being advanced as a theoretical proof (inadequate) or as a practical postulate needed for moral agency. Do not conflate moral justification with theoretical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith as habitus grounded adequately for its practical design
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith (as habitus, not as actus) is the moral attitude of Reason to assume as true that which is necessary to presuppose as condition of the possibility of the highest moral final purpose, although its possibility or impossibility cannot be comprehended by us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat faith as a stable moral disposition justified by the requirements of practical Reason for pursuing moral ends. Scoring note: faith is 'adequate' when it serves the practical design (moral final purpose) even without theoretical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish faith from credulity and opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Faith that refers to particular objects which are not objects of possible knowledge or opinion is moral; credulity refers especially to historical matters and is belief without adequate ground. Unbelief that denies validity to rational Ideas is dogmatical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a belief has rational practical grounding (faith) versus being mere credulity (ungrounded acceptance of testimony) or dogmatic unbelief (rejecting rational Ideas outright). Anti-pattern: calling moral faith 'credulity' when it serves a practical rational function.

rubrics_metrics.name: All belief must be grounded on facts for non-groundlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: All belief must in the first place be grounded upon facts, if it is not to be completely groundless; belief derived from proofs can be knowledge (for theoretical cognition) or faith (for practical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proofs by whether they rest on facts (empirical or practical effects). Distinguish whether resulting assent is knowledge (theoretical) or faith (practical). Do not accept arguments that lack any factual or practical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of ontological and cosmological proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The ontological proof (from the concept of the Being most real) and the metaphysico-cosmological proof (from necessity of some being) are sophistries that cannot pass from the schools into the world or influence common understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat purely conceptual or purely metaphysical deductions of God's existence with skepticism; they fail to provide determinate, convincing concepts for ordinary understanding. Anti-pattern: relying solely on a priori conceptual necessity to prove empirical or practical matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits of physico-teleological proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof derived from the purposes of nature (physical Teleology) can guide Reason to think of an intelligent World-Cause but cannot supply a determinate concept of God; its persuasive force often mingles with moral grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physico-teleological arguments to motivate thinking about an intelligent cause, but do not treat them as furnishing a complete theological concept. Recognize when aesthetic/admiration responses are covertly doing the persuasive work rather than empirical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral teleology supplies the determinate concept needed for Theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral Teleology, based on the concept of freedom and the demands of practical Reason, leads to a determinate concept of the supreme Cause (God) appropriate for Theology because it supplies the final purpose and attributes (e.g., omniscience, omnipotence) required for the moral final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking a theological concept adequate for religion (practical use), prioritize moral arguments grounded in the demands of practical Reason rather than empirical teleology or pure speculation. Scoring note: moral teleology suffices for practical conviction though not for speculative cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious applying empirical Categories to the supersensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories (e.g., causality) that determine objects of sense cannot cognize supersensible beings theoretically; applying them to God leaves the concept empty rather than informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ascribing spatio-temporal or sensory-based predicates (place, extension, duration) to supersensible beings as if they were empirical objects. Use analogical thinking only for practical reference, not as theoretical cognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy permitted for practical (ethical) cognition but not theoretical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: According to analogy of an Understanding we can think a supersensible being without intending to cognize it theoretically; this allows an 'Ethical Theology' (theology grounded in moral ideas) while a Theological Ethic (morality grounded in theology) is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In constructing religious or theological claims for moral purposes, use analogy to attribute functional properties to God insofar as they serve practical Reason. Do not claim such analogical attributions as theoretical knowledge of God's nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theology's role is subjective for Religion (practical use of Reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theology is not needed for extension/correction of cognition of nature or theory, but subjectively for Religion—that is, for the practical or moral use of Reason where the moral argument provides sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theological systems by their capacity to support moral duty and the final purpose of practical Reason, not by their contribution to speculative natural knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral proof vs physical proof: different principles and distinct domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical Teleology and moral proof are heterogeneous and can only furnish two different kinds of proof; attempting to derive one from the other is unavailing for what is to be proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing arguments, keep track of whether they rest on 'nature' (empirical purposiveness) or 'freedom' (moral causality). Do not conflate the justificatory domains; each establishes different kinds of conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a determinate theological concept
rubrics_metrics.description: For a concept of the original Being available for Theology, natural properties required include Omniscience, Omnipotence, Omnipresence, etc., thought as bound up with the moral final purpose which is infinite and adequate to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proposing a theological concept intended to serve as a basis for moral final purposes, ensure it includes the totality of perfections compatible with intelligence. Anti-pattern: inferring uniqueness or maximal attributes of a deity purely from limited empirical signs of purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper attitude toward assumptions added for practical use
rubrics_metrics.description: One may arbitrarily add assumptions (e.g., uniqueness of the Deity) for better employment of Reason, but such additions cannot be regarded as proved by purely theoretical grounds and should be acknowledged as pragmatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when adopting pragmatic/theoretical assumptions to make Reason more serviceable; do not present such interpolations as proven truths. Scoring note: clarity about when one is assuming vs proving increases intellectual honesty.
